title: Sri Lanka, Japan step up efforts to address investor concerns and develop export-oriented industrial corridor | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 05:22
-     - 36

The Board of Investment of Sri Lanka (BOI) has stepped up efforts to address operational challenges faced by Japanese investors, with the fifth working-level meeting of the Sri Lanka–Japan Business Environment Committee providing a platform for companies to raise concerns directly with relevant government agencies.

The quarterly meeting brought together representatives of the Embassy of Japan, Japan External Trade Organisation (JETRO), Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry (JCCI), Japanese companies operating in Sri Lanka, the BOI and other relevant government institutions.

Japanese companies were given the opportunity to present issues affecting their respective operations, with government agencies providing clarifications and responses during the discussions.

The concerns covered a broad range of sectors, reflecting the diversity of Japanese investment in Sri Lanka. These included manufacturing and industrial production, consumer and health products, value-added trade, environmental services, infrastructure, logistics and energy.

The BOI said discussions between Government officials and Japanese business representatives were productive and constructive, reaffirming the importance of sustained dialogue and coordination in addressing investor concerns.

The meeting also reiterated the BOI’s role as the principal liaison between investors and the Government, with participants stressing the Committee’s importance in identifying and resolving operational issues, whilst strengthening bilateral economic cooperation.

Meanwhile, the first meeting of the Sri Lanka–Japan Joint Working Group on Export-Oriented Industrial Corridor Development was held concurrently.

The establishment of the working group marks a further step in broadening the focus of Sri Lanka-Japan economic cooperation beyond individual investor concerns towards potential industrial and export-oriented development.

title: ABC Trade and Investment signs MoU with All-China Environment Federation | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 05:20
-     - 18

ABC Trade and Investment Ltd., Director/CEO Amalrajah Jayaseelan (right) with All-China Environment Federation Secretary-General the Belt and Road Eco-Industry Cooperation Working Committee Shi Xiang

ABC Trade and Investments Ltd., has entered into a strategic Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the All-China Environment Federation (ACEF). 

The partnership establishes a collaborative framework aimed at accelerating new-energy development, water management, and environmental protection projects across Sri Lanka.  

The agreement bridges advanced Chinese engineering capabilities, equipment, technical expertise, and investment resources with ABC Trade and Investments’ local operational strength, market insight, and project implementation skills. By pairing international technology with on-the-ground execution, the initiative is designed to address Sri Lanka’s long-term environmental and civil infrastructure priorities.

A statement said ABC Trade and Investments’ as a leading home-grown conglomerate in Sri Lanka’s ICT distribution and diversified business landscape.

The MoU signing took place during the China–Sri Lanka Environmental and Energy Exchange and Cooperation Meeting at the Nondescripts Cricket Club Grounds in Colombo, held under the theme “Empower Green Development, Jointly Build a New Pattern of China–Sri Lanka Environmental and Energy Industry.”  

ABC Trade and Investment Ltd., Director/CEO Amalrajah Jayaseelan said: “ACEF gives us access to a wider network of Chinese environmental and engineering capabilities, while we bring an understanding of local requirements, regulations, and implementation realities. Our focus is now on identifying the right technologies, adapting them to local conditions, and developing practical projects that address real needs in water, clean energy, and environmental management.”  

The scope of the cooperation spans a broad spectrum of environmental applications. Priority areas identified for immediate project development include integrated urban and rural water supply and drainage systems, domestic sewage treatment upgrades, industrial park wastewater management, village drinking water purification, distributed renewable energy installations, and clean energy systems linked directly to water infrastructure.   

The partnership leverages the complementary strengths of both organisations. ACEF brings a vast network of Chinese enterprises operating across environmental protection, water engineering, renewable energy, and EPC (Engineering, Procurement, and Construction) investment. ABC Trade and Investments contributes a nationwide service infrastructure and specialised expertise through its Water Science Division, which provides end-to-end management spanning consultation, solution design, equipment supply, installation, commissioning, and long-term Operation and Maintenance (OandM).  

The MoU establishes a structured, long-term cooperation framework under which individual commercial and technical projects will be identified, evaluated, and contracted independently. By matching proven environmental technologies with local realities, ABC Trade and Investments and ACEF aim to build practical, scalable infrastructure solutions that support sustainable development throughout Sri Lanka.

title: CPA Australia impressed with growth; sees bigger potential for SL | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 04:44
-     - 25

CPA Australia Board President and Chair Prof.Dale Pinto - Pic by Lasantha Kumara

By Nisthar Cassim

CPA Australia President Prof Dale recently identified Sri Lanka as one of its most exciting growth markets.

This assessment is based on the fact that the world famous CPA qualification has gained a lot of traction in Sri Lanka following the opening of the Sri Lanka Liaison Office as well as strong partnership with government, universities and employers as well as signing of pathway agreements with both the CA Sri Lanka and the CMA Sri Lanka.

CPA Australia is a professional accounting body in Australia, originally founded as the “Incorporated Institute of Accountants” in 1886. CPA Australia is one of the world’s largest accounting bodies, with a global membership of over 176,000 members across over 100 countries. One third of the membership is outside Australia.

 “We have built a vibrant member community. We have gone from 400 members two years ago to 600 which is a 50% growth in a short period of time,” explained Dale in an interview with the Daily FT along with CPA Australia’s Country Representative in Sri Lanka Dinuk Hettiaratchchi.

“When I first became CPA Australia President and visited Sri Lanka, what really struck me was not just the numbers of members, but the quality of the members that were. These were people who were not just concerned about accounting, but how to become better accountants and how to grow Sri Lanka. This optimism gives me tremendous confidence,” said Dale, who was in Sri Lanka recently to participate in CPA’s 140th anniversary celebrations.

Sri Lanka has exceptional talent and CPA Australia is committed to helping that talent succeed not only here but across the Asia Pacific region and the world

CPA Australia is optimistic about Sri Lanka given the quality of the talent in the country. “Sri Lanka’s strength in many ways is its people. The people there have got a thirst for knowledge. They have got a global mindset, and they want to make the world a better place, and that sounds a bit cheesy, but it is actually true because I hear it from enough people that they can’t be all colluding with each other.”

President Dale said Sri Lanka has an excellent opportunity to become a regional hub for finance, shared services and professional expertise. “High-quality finance professionals can help attract international investment through better governance and transparency,” CPA Australia President emphasised. 

“Sri Lanka has exceptional talent and CPA Australia is committed to helping that talent succeed not only here but across the Asia Pacific region and the world,” Dale added.

Challenges to global accounting profession

In terms of challenges to the global accounting profession, CPA Australia President identified Artificial Intelligence and cyber security as the biggest ones facing not just accounting but everyone. Other challenges include talent attraction and retention; ethics, regulatory complexity where different rules apply in different jurisdictions; climate and sustainability reporting that many countries are requiring and geopolitical upheavals and resultant economic volatilities. 

“With all of those challenges, people, and that is whether it is clients or businesses or government, look for trusted advisors. That is where the role of accountants comes in, not just to provide financial statements, but to help them navigate uncertainty, to help them understand AI, to help them decode regulatory complexity, to help them explain different cultures, and that’s where a body like CPA Australia comes in. Because we are in 100 countries, we can share what we know from our evidence works in each jurisdiction with our members,” emphasised President Dale.

“The future accountant will combine technical excellence with technology, ethics and leadership. Those who embrace lifelong learning will not simply adapt to change. They will lead,” said Dale adding “The accounting profession has evolved from bookkeepers to business advisers and now to architects of trust in a digital economy.”

High-quality finance professionals can help attract international investment through better governance and transparency

CPA Australia, which is a  member of the International Federation of Accountants (IFAC), is expanding partnership with global and regional accounting bodies with South Asia Federation of Accountants (SAFA) being the most recent. “All of the challenges that we are facing now are external to all of our bodies. So whether it is AI, sustainability, regulatory complexity, geopolitical uncertainty, these are external forces, and when you are dealing with challenges in that context, you can’t solve them unilaterally. You have to collaborate.”

Dale also explained CPA Australia’s Thought Leadership initiative to develop future leaders. It does a number of reports including Asia Pacific Small Business Survey; Business Technology Report, ESG research and AI insights.

“Our priorities continue to promote regional mobility, and via Member Recognition Agreements (MRAs), CPA Australia fosters greater collaboration to help SMEs adopt digital technologies, to promote ethical use of AI, and to support sustainable economic growth.

MRAs is where members of the parties to the agreement can become members of the other. For example a member of CA Sri Lanka can join CPA Australia. They don’t have to do the CPA Australia program but as per the agreement, enjoys some reductions. 

“We want to make sure that there is genuine mobility and there’s genuine benefits for both parties. So we don’t just do it to get members into our body. We do it so members from our body can also go there. Otherwise, we don’t go into the agreement if it’s one-sided,” Dale explained. 

“We are not standing still. We are undertaking what’s called the Learning Evolution program, and that is a major change to our CPA program and it’s related to CPDs, that is to include things like AI, sustainability, and emerging things that business professionals need to know,” explained Dale. 

He referred to CPA Australia’s value proposition “partners for progress” ensuring members have got the educational resources, practical toolkits and checklists to help them. “Because if you are a small business, for example, your main job is conducting a business, and so our job as a professional body is to help them in practical ways whenever they have an issue.”

Amidst multiple challenges, whether it is clients or businesses or government, look for trusted advisors. That’s where the role of accountants comes in, not just to provide financial statements, but to help them navigate uncertainty

CPA Australia has a very successful initiative called “Build Days” bringing members and partners together to develop solutions. The more recent one was held in Sydney on AI tools. CPA Australia is also planning to establish an AI hub, with resources and practical ideas. 

Following are excerpts of the interview.

Q: AI is relatively new to professionals. What is the biggest drawback in terms of members adopting AI?

A: Members are more accounting driven, but they also may have been empowered by AI. We are trying to teach the responsible usage of AI, which is the ethical use of it. The second thing is to actually teach people how to use it in their business. I think the biggest fear is you know there’s a phrase called “AI where people think it’s going to replace me. So because of that, what do I do? I put the fence up. I don’t want to know about it, but in fact, what it does is it gets rid of all the routine tasks like invoice processing or data processing, and it frees up the accountant’s time to do analysis and also to become a strategic business partner to tell the story behind the numbers. So it is a higher level of thinking, but that is a different mindset. So accountants are going from being bookkeepers to being business advisors. That’s a big change. So we have to bring people on the journey and tell them, look, you don’t have to worry. Your work will change, but you are going to do more interesting work in a more valuable way. But that’s a journey. Technology may replace tasks. It will not replace trust.

Q: What’s the real advantage a company would have if you have a CPA member, What’s the value they bring in?

A: I think my simple phrase would be, it is a recognition of being a trusted advisor who is educated in the current rules, but also the ethical practice of those rules. So we pride ourselves. We got one word in our crest, which is integrity. So to me, if you look at a CPA Australia, you should think of a trusted advisor.

Q: How do you respond to some of the failures by accounting professionals and firms?

A: The first line of defence is obviously education. We try to educate people on doing the right thing. But if people don’t do the right thing, we have got a very strong and robust professional conduct regime, and we have penalties that can go up to $100,000 in Australia, and you can lose your membership and right to practice. So that can be an existential threat. Now we don’t like to use that, but in cases where people have been behaving egregiously, you have to because otherwise all the people who are doing the right thing get tarred with the same brush. This always happens in any big community.

Technology may replace tasks. It will not replace trust

You are always going to have outliers, so you have to deal with them. We are doing our best to do that. We have had well publicised cases in Australia of big firms, which, although they are not our members, still impacts the profession. When you are dealing with trust, it is an easy thing to lose and it is a hard thing to regain. On our website we regularly update all the professional conduct actions. So that’s visible for people to see. Once a year, we have to appear before Parliament, and they ask us questions, and that’s on the public record on how many people we have sanctioned, how many people we have terminated, what fines were imposed. So in that sense, there is transparency and accountability. There will be some cases where, because of the nature of the people involved, the names won’t be published, but the general trends and the cases and the incidents and how we are going about it-that is all transparent.

Q: Where do you see the world is heading?

A: The world’s in a very volatile and dynamic phase. Volatile because of geopolitical considerations. Dynamic because of rapidly evolving phenomena like AI. We have got almost like the perfect storm at the moment, but like any storm, I think the weather passes, and then you have got to make sure that you ride with the waves as they are passing you and try to negotiate as best you can. You stay true to your principles such as integrity, professional standards, and acting in the public interest. Those for us are the three features which define a profession. Now, if we lose that, then we won’t exist, no matter what the conditions are outside. We have to stay true to that. But we have to respond to all of these things because we have obviously got members and the public to serve. So that philosophy is applicable whether you are dealing with a global economy or a regional economy.

I came across two things. One was AI dread, where people thought the world’s going to end.

and another one was called apocalypticist, which combines apocalypse with optimists. So it’s like glass half full, and I’m that person. Whether you are talking globally or whether you are talking regionally or whether you’re talking nationally, it is the same thing manifested in different ways, and there might be different aspects of it. But ultimately, you know the world changes, the world pivots. So I’m one of the apocalyptomists. You have to continually change.

Q: What’s your kind of advice for emerging economies like Sri Lanka?  

A: One is to foster this professionalism and profession and also to get things right.

There are a number of things. One is obviously learning from the lessons of others, collaborating with others where it makes sense to do that. There’s basic principles of trust, which include transparency. I call it “my five”, which is simplicity, keeping things as simple as you can, so you don’t overcomplicate laws. For example, certainty would be my second thing, where you know businesses need certainty to invest and foreign direct investment, same thing. Then I call it equity. There needs to be a sense of fairness, so that’s important. The fourth one is neutrality, where I think there shouldn’t be any distortions. So you know it shouldn’t produce incentives for me to behave in a certain way. The last one comes back to the government, which is efficiency. So making sure administration costs are minimised and compliance costs to businesses, therefore, are minimised. Now that all sounds very obvious and simple, which it is conceptually, but to do it practically is very challenging.

The future accountant will combine technical excellence with technology, ethics and leadership. Those who embrace lifelong learning will not simply adapt to change. They will lead. The accounting profession has evolved from bookkeepers to business advisers and now to architects of trust in a digital economy

Q: What’s coming ahead for CPAs for the entire region as an organisation?

A: We are embarking on a major project called Learning Evolution. Yeah. So that’s evolving our educational offerings. That is the biggest investment we’ve got at the moment. Okay. The second thing is AI. AI is really how we adopt it within the organisation, but how do we deploy it to our members, so they can help their clients as well. The third big one for us is actually the future of the profession. We are making sure we can continue to attract and retain the next generation of accountants. Accounting is seen as not being exciting, not paying a lot, and going to be replaced by AI. The demand for accountants is still high because machines can’t sign off. So humans are still accountable. So paradoxically, demand’s up, but supply’s going down because people are going away from accounting. So I think they would be the three big challenges we’ve got amongst those other things of sustainability, reporting, and geopolitical. But they’re second order compared to these first three.

Q: How do you be relevant to or attractive to the younger generation?

A: CPA has got a campaign called “Three Letters to Limitless” which is CPA. The Three Letters to Limitless is trying to explain to people the limitless careers a course in accounting can give. Not just financial accountant or management accountant or auditor or tax-they are the traditional ones but forensic accountant, data analyst, sustainability accountant. We have developed 24 of these exciting careers. We are trying to sell that to show people, and some of them haven’t even got the word accountant in it, which actually helps. There’s a stigma with being an accountant is boring. We are showing people how technologies like AI can actually free them from doing the routine work and get them involved in more strategic value adding.

title: Southern business chambers press Treasury on barriers to growth | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 05:38
-     - 9

The medium and large-scale businesses have taken their concerns over mounting operational and policy challenges directly to the Treasury, with Southern Province business chambers seeking time-bound solutions from the Government.

The issues were raised at a meeting held yesterday (7) at the Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry following a request by the Southern Province Chambers Forum. Finance and Planning Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando and Economic Development Deputy Minister Nishantha Jayaweera chaired the discussion.

Representatives of several business associations affiliated with the Forum presented their concerns and challenges in detail, while also putting forward proposals aimed at addressing the constraints faced by businesses.

Jayaweera said the Government had reached policy-level agreement to address many of the issues raised, with discussions to follow on the timeframe required to implement the proposed solutions.

Dr. Fernando said several measures had already been initiated to respond to the concerns presented by the business community.

The meeting was significant as businesses continue to push for a more predictable and enabling operating environment, with regulatory, taxation, customs and other administrative bottlenecks affecting investment and expansion decisions.

Officials from the Finance Ministry, Sri Lanka Customs and the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) also participated, bringing key revenue and regulatory agencies into the discussion.

Business representatives welcomed the Government’s quick response to their request, expressing appreciation to the two Deputy Ministers for facilitating the meeting within a short period.

title: Petition alleges fundamental rights violated over unheard 22nd Amendment challenge | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 05:37
-     - 9

A fundamental rights petition has been filed before the Supreme Court seeking a declaration that the rights of two petitioners were violated after the Court allegedly failed to hear a petition challenging the 22nd Amendment Bill to the Constitution presented to Parliament by the Government.

The petition was filed by Union of National Organisations Convenor Dulara Gunathilake and retired Sri Lanka Air Force officer Shantha Jayathilake.

The petitioners state that Gunathilake had previously filed a petition before the Supreme Court challenging the 22nd Amendment Bill, but that the petition was not called in open Court for examination. They have requested the Court to determine that their fundamental rights were violated as a result of the omission.

The petitioners have also requested an interim order preventing the Court’s determination on the 22nd Amendment Bill from being communicated to the Speaker of Parliament until the present petition is heard and a final judgment delivered.

title: Australia and Sri Lanka strengthen partnership on electoral integrity | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 05:37
-     - 10

Australia and Sri Lanka have taken another step forward in their longstanding partnership, with the Australian Electoral Commission and the Election Commission of Sri Lanka signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in Colombo on 2 September.

Strong, trusted election systems are fundamental to vibrant and well-functioning democracies. They ensure democratic institutions reflect their communities, respond to the needs of their people, and maintain public confidence.

As Indian Ocean neighbours and two of the region’s most vibrant democracies, Australia and Sri Lanka are natural partners. Both countries share a commitment to credible electoral processes, strong public institutions, and democratic governance.

The MoU will deepen practical cooperation between the two electoral commissions, creating opportunities to share expertise, exchange experience, and learn from each other on election management and administration.

Australian High Commissioner to Sri Lanka Matthew Duckworth said: “Strong election systems are the bedrock of our democracies. They give citizens confidence that their voices count, that their governments reflect the community’s aspirations and that their institutions serve them. As Indian Ocean neighbours and two of the region’s most vibrant democracies, Australia and Sri Lanka are natural partners. This agreement brings together two respected electoral institutions to share expertise, learn from each other and strengthen the systems that underpin our democracies. As Australia and Sri Lanka approach 80 years of partnership, this is another practical example of our countries working together to build strong institutions and deliver for our people.”

The signing was attended by Australian High Commissioner Duckworth, Australian Electoral Commission Acting Assistant Commissioner Melinda Vernon, Director – International Engagement Joanne Ridolfi, Election Commission of Sri Lanka Chairman R.M.A.L. Ratnayake, members of the Commission, General of Elections Commissioner Rasika Peiris, and senior officials from both organisations.

title: UN delegation calls on President’s Chief of Staff | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 05:33
-     - 9

The United Nations (UN) has pledged support for Sri Lanka’s efforts to resettle people displaced by Cyclone Ditwah, while discussions with the Government have also focused on preparations for potential future disasters amid El Niño conditions.

UN Resident Coordinator Marc-André Franche held discussions yesterday with Chief of Staff to the President Prabath Chandrakeerthi at the Presidential Secretariat, with the Government’s post-Ditwah resettlement program receiving particular attention.

Chandrakeerthi briefed Franche on the Government’s plans to resettle people who lost their homes as a result of the cyclone and outlined measures being prepared to respond to potential disasters associated with El Niño conditions.

The discussions come as Sri Lanka continues to address the humanitarian and reconstruction fallout from Ditwah, while seeking to strengthen its preparedness for increasingly complex climate-related risks.

Franche said the UN was ready to provide the necessary assistance to support the successful implementation of the Government’s resettlement and disaster preparedness programs.

The meeting also focused on strengthening cooperation between the Government and the UN in responding to future emergencies and building resilience against climate-related shocks.

UN Partnerships and Development Finance Specialist Azam Bakeer Markar and UN Sri Lanka Humanitarian and Resilience Officer Wagisha Perera also participated in the meeting.

title: Ex-Minister Jayakody’s corruption case postponed to 5 Oct. | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 05:31
-     - 11

The Colombo High Court yesterday ordered that further examination of evidence in the corruption case against former Power and Energy Minister Kumara Jayakody be taken up on 5 October. 

The Bribery Commission alleges Jayakody, while serving as Procurement Manager at the Lanka Fertiliser Company in 2014, caused a loss of over Rs. 8.8 million to the Government by conducting the procurement process for carpeting the company’s Hunupitiya warehouse complex in a manner that gave undue benefit to a private company.

Testifying under the direction of Bribery Commission Assistant Director General Asitha Anthony, former Lanka Fertiliser Company Chairman Buddhika Ruwan Madihahewa said D.S. Construction was selected for the work and paid more than Rs. 8.8 million as an advance under a performance bond. He said he approved the payment after reviewing documents from the Procurement and Finance Divisions confirming procedures had been followed.

Madihahewa admitted the carpeting work was never carried out, and that raw materials, including stones brought for the project, remained on company premises. He said only Rs. 2,214,921 was later recovered under the performance bond.

A legal officer from the National Audit Office also gave evidence during the hearing.

title: 60 wars now active, highest since WWII: UN Rights Chief | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 05:30
-     - 12

United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk

United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk told the UN Human Rights Council’s 63rd Session that more than 60 wars involving at least one state are currently active, the highest count since World War Two, warning of declining respect for international law and a weakening commitment to the UN Charter.

He flagged renewed US-Iran hostilities as destabilising the Gulf region, calling the crisis avoidable and urging an immediate return to negotiations. On Ukraine, now in its fifth year of Russian invasion, Türk cited rising civilian casualties and intensifying energy-infrastructure strikes, and voiced concern over reports that Russian autonomous drones killed three Ukrainians last month, noting Kyiv has also tested similar systems. He renewed calls for an international ban on weapons that can kill without human decision-making.

“There is only one way out of this madness: peace negotiations that respect the UN Charter,” Türk said.

He urged governments to strengthen domestic accountability, back the International Criminal Court, and expand use of universal jurisdiction to prosecute atrocity crimes where national courts cannot or will not act. “The tragedy of conflict has touched almost all our lives,” he said, citing lasting effects on displacement, public health and the environment.

title: AfD wins first place in German State election; a first for far right since WWII | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 8 September 2026 05:28
-     - 12

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) surged into first place in Saxony-Anhalt’s State election on Sunday, exit polls showed, putting the far-right party within reach of power at the state level for the first time since World War Two.

The AfD won 44% of the vote, short of an overall majority, but dealt a heavy blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives, reflecting deep unpopularity of the ruling federal coalition. Turnout was 77%, according to broadcaster ZDF.

The AfD is already Germany’s most popular party at the national level, polling at 28% in a recent INSA poll, ahead of the conservatives on 20%. It is seeking to secure a foothold in Saxony-Anhalt to advance its national agenda, which includes heavy restrictions on immigration, restoring ties with Russia, cutting support to Ukraine and quitting the euro.

“We have made history in this country,” said Ulrich Siegmund, AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, who has repeatedly cast a state victory as a first step toward securing national power in federal elections due in 2029. “The people have made it absolutely clear that they finally want political change and, above all, they have shown that they want it with us,” he said.

Germany’s mainstream parties have all refused to work with the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist by the local office of Germany’s domestic intelligence service. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which looked set to clear the threshold to enter parliament, has floated the idea of Saxony-Anhalt being run by a non-partisan state premier relying on shifting majorities, including AfD votes. Siegmund rejected the idea as a “mess,” ruling out any arrangement that would prevent the AfD from delivering on its promise of change. “If push comes to shove, there will simply be new elections,” he said.
